title: The floodgates are open after another Chinese company lands a reusable rocket
gist: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 achieved China's first land-based reusable-rocket booster landing just 40 days after CASC's Long March 10B pulled off an ocean-net recovery, signaling China is compressing the reusability timeline the US took a decade to achieve while SpaceX's Falcon 9 approaches retirement.

insights.claim: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 achieved China's first successful land-based first-stage booster recovery using landing legs on August 18-19, 2026, coming about 40 days after CASC's Long March 10B achieved China's first booster recovery of any kind via an offshore net catch on July 10.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Two distinct successful reusable-booster recovery methods from two different Chinese companies within 40 days signals a rapidly maturing domestic launch industry that could compress the cost gap with SpaceX within a few years.
insights.quote: This mission marks China's first-ever successful recovery attempt of the first stage of an orbital-class launch vehicle using landing legs, and China's first successful booster recovery on land
insights.locator: MISSION SUCCESS | ZhuQue-3 Y2 Reusable Launch Vehicle

insights.claim: It took the US ten years between SpaceX's first orbital-class booster landing in 2015 and Blue Origin's first successful landing, while China achieved two different companies' successful booster recoveries within about 40 days of each other in 2026.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: China's dual-track state-and-commercial approach appears to be compressing a reusability-adoption timeline that took the US a decade, a structural competitiveness signal for the global launch industry.
insights.locator: It took 10 years for a second US launch company, Blue Origin

insights.claim: LandSpace plans to fly each Zhuque-3 booster at least 20 times, and Chinese officials project the country's two largest planned satellite mega-constellations, Guowang and Qianfan, will require 700 to 800 rocket launches over the next seven to ten years.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: This represents a massive addressable domestic launch-demand pool that could underwrite Chinese reusable-rocket economics independent of Western commercial customers.
insights.locator: Chinese officials project the country's two largest constellations

insights.claim: The Zhuque-3 booster closely resembles SpaceX's Falcon 9 in design (grid fins, landing legs) but runs on methane rather than kerosene, aligning with the broader industry shift toward methane engines also used in SpaceX's Starship.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Methane-fuel convergence across US and Chinese next-generation rockets suggests methane is becoming the default propellant choice for reusable launch vehicles industry-wide.
insights.locator: The Zhuque-3 booster bears a striking resemblance to SpaceX's Falcon 9

insights.claim: China is developing a Starship-class fully reusable super-heavy rocket, the Long March 9, but it will not fly until sometime after 2030, meaning China's near-term reusable capability is concentrated in medium-lift vehicles rather than super-heavy lift.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Delineates the timeline gap between China's near-term medium-lift reusability wins and its longer-term super-heavy ambitions, relevant for forecasting when China could directly compete with Starship-class payload capacity.
insights.locator: China is working on a Starship-like rocket called the Long March 9

insights.claim: SpaceX is looking to wind down commercial availability of the Falcon 9 rocket after 2028 in favor of Starship, but Starship remains experimental with a history of schedule delays, potentially forcing SpaceX to reconsider the Falcon 9's retirement.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Any further Starship delays extend the window during which Falcon 9 remains the commercial workhorse, and also the window of opportunity for emerging competitors to capture launch market share.
insights.locator: SpaceX is looking to wind down the Falcon 9 rocket soon

insights.claim: Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Firefly Aerospace (working with Northrop Grumman) are developing reusable rockets that could make first flights in the next couple of years, potentially becoming the third US company to land an orbital-class booster.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: These companies represent the medium-to-heavy launch market's potential beneficiaries once Falcon 9 winds down, a watchlist for investors tracking the next wave of reusable-launch entrants.
insights.locator: Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Relativity Space, and Firefly Aerospace

insights.claim: Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which appeared poised for a breakout year after its first booster reflight, is now grounded following a launch-pad explosion in Florida in May 2026.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Removes a near-term reusable-rocket competitor from active service, at least temporarily benefiting SpaceX and Chinese entrants competing for the same medium-to-heavy launch demand.
insights.locator: the rocket is now grounded after an explosion on the launch pad

insights.claim: United Launch Alliance has no near-term plans for a reusable rocket architecture, and China's collective launch cadence (state-owned CASC plus commercial rivals) is still only about half of SpaceX's, though achieved entirely with expendable rockets to date.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: China's launch-cadence deficit versus SpaceX could narrow materially once reusability scales, while ULA remains structurally disadvantaged on per-launch cost among major US providers.
insights.locator: The other major US launch provider, United Launch Alliance
